Messages.Author: Eric Topp
Messages.Body:
The key drawback of a "pure" rush deck (i.e. one with no reaction
capability) is that it is a combo deck. If you draw a hand of combat cards
but no Bum's Rush, Ambush or Haven Uncovered, you cannot enter combat. If
you draw a hand of BR/Ambush/HC and no combat cards, you can enter combat
but at a disadvantage.

I used a pure rush deck (a Torn Signpost - Immortal Grapple deck constructed
by James Hamblin listed at http://www.dejanews.com/getdoc.xp?AN=376738853)
at my last tournament. The first round I brought Beast out of my crypt.
Because Beast does not require a card to enter combat, I swept the table.
The other three rounds, Beast stayed in my crypt and I did not earn a single
victory point. My combat monsters watched helplessly as my predator's
minions snuck past at +1 stealth.

A rush deck that relies on BR/Ambush/HC and lacks *any* intercept ability is
doomed to failure.
--
Eric Topp
eric...@interact.net.au

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Eric Topp wrote:
"The key drawback of a "pure" rush deck (i.e. one with no reaction
capability) is that it is a combo deck. If you draw a hand of combat cards but
no Bum's Rush, Ambush or Haven Uncovered, you cannot enter combat. If you draw
a hand of BR/Ambush/HC and no combat cards, you can enter combat but at a
disadvantage."

While having to rely on drawing get into combat cards can be a problem, your
impression of the Pure Rush deck is simply incorrect. Yes, you need to have a
Rush card in your hand to get the deck going, but with the right mix of cards
(about 4 Haven/12 Bum's Rush in a 90 card deck), you really shouldn't have any
trouble getting into combat when you need to. Sure, occasionally you will get
a totally screwy shuffle and never get to pick a Rush card, but this is pretty
rare. All you need is a good mix of the appropriate cards, some deck cycling
(Barrens/Dreams/Fragment), the knowledge of what and when to discard, and this
hypothetical problem will have very little, if any effect on your game.

"I used a pure rush deck (a Torn Signpost - Immortal Grapple deck constructed
by James Hamblin listed at http://www.dejanews.com/getdoc.xp?AN=376738853)
at my last tournament. The first round I brought Beast out of my crypt. Because
Beast does not require a card to enter combat, I swept the table. The other
three rounds, Beast stayed in my crypt and I did not earn a single victory
point. My combat monsters watched helplessly as my predator's minions snuck
past at +1 stealth."

As I have played against James's combat decks many, many times, I can only
assume that A) You had completely improbable shuffles or B) You had trouble
because you were using a deck that you didn't design, and as such, didn't
really know how to play it real well. Pure rush decks do just fine, even
without permanent Rush characters like Beast. At Origins, my Rush deck (which
has been posted here numerous times and is in the Nosferatu Newsletters) did
very well, sweeping one table and getting into the finals, never had any
trouble at all getting into combat, and had no permamnent Rush characters
whatsoever. Just the appropriate mix of Rush cards and hand cycling ability.

"A rush deck that relies on BR/Ambush/HC and lacks *any* intercept ability is
doomed to failure."

This is completely incorrect. My pure rush decks have done very well in
tournaments. James's have done very well in tournaments. Josh Duffin's have
done very well in tournaments. I'm sure other folks have as well. Having no
intercept just means you need to get into combat with Rush cards. Again, with
the appropriate proportion of cards and some deck cycling ability, the Rush
deck should, and will do just fine.

Why you did poorly with James's deck, I have no idea. Did you change the mix
of cards at all? Did you get incredibly bad shuffles and never discard? Did
you wait around and try to block rather than pre-emptively Rushing? Did you
constantly sit next to Fortitude anti-combat decks?

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Eric Topp wrote:
>
> The key drawback of a "pure" rush deck (i.e. one with no reaction
> capability) is that it is a combo deck. If you draw a hand of combat cards
> but no Bum's Rush, Ambush or Haven Uncovered, you cannot enter combat. If
> you draw a hand of BR/Ambush/HC and no combat cards, you can enter combat
> but at a disadvantage.

This "critical hand jam" does happen occasionally, but it can be helped:
by discarding _every_ turn, by playing any master cards available, and
by making sure you have enough get-into-combat cards. With 16/90 (12
Bum's Rush, 4 Haven Uncovered), it's rather unlikely that you'll get
none of these cards in, say, your first 9 cards, assuming you discard on
the first two turns:

74 * 73 * 72 * 71 * 70 * 69 * 68 * 67 * 66
-- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- = 0.15649
90 89 88 87 86 85 84 83 82

So 85% of the time you'll have a rush card in your opening hand, or
after a couple of discards. Once you get into combat, you'll cycle
cards like mad, and life will be good. I mean, you should never really
have a hand devoid of combat cards, since a good rush combat deck should
have three things: good combat cards, get-into-combat cards, and useful
masters.

What to do the 15% of the time you don't get a rush card? The best you
can; play as many cards as you can. Put potence masters on your
opponent's vampires if you have to get something out of your hand. This
situation is tough, and I have lost games due to it (when I had a fast
predator), but that doesn't make the deck any less viable. Everyone
gets hand jammed every once and a while.
There's no need to make sweeping generalizations about the general
effectiveness of the entire strategy. If you find you need to put more
rush cards in the deck to prevent this sort of thing from happening, go
right ahead.

> I used a pure rush deck (a Torn Signpost - Immortal Grapple deck constructed
> by James Hamblin listed at http://www.dejanews.com/getdoc.xp?AN=376738853)
> at my last tournament.

I'm sort of perplexed at your description of the deck as a "Torn
Signpost / Immortal Grapple deck". It seems possible to me that your
description of having "no combat cards" meant that you had no IG or no
TS in your hand. But the combat can be effective without those cards.
Not everyone uses S:CE, and it's likely that either your predator or
your prey is either playing a deck without it, or at the very least has
a weak vampire without the right discipline. So, no IG? No problem.
Having no Torn Signpost is not even a problem at all! That's what the
_other_ cards are for! You know, Blur, Undead Strength, Pushing the
Limit, Fists of Death... need I go on?

Doomed to failure? Hardly.

James

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Eric Topp (eric...@interact.net.au) wrote:
: The key drawback of a "pure" rush deck (i.e. one with no reaction
: capability) is that it is a combo deck. If you draw a hand of combat cards
: but no Bum's Rush, Ambush or Haven Uncovered, you cannot enter combat. If
: you draw a hand of BR/Ambush/HC and no combat cards, you can enter combat
: but at a disadvantage.

: I used a pure rush deck (a Torn Signpost - Immortal Grapple deck constructed

: by James Hamblin listed at http://www.dejanews.com/getdoc.xp?AN=376738853)

: at my last tournament. The first round I brought Beast out of my crypt.

: Because Beast does not require a card to enter combat, I swept the table.
: The other three rounds, Beast stayed in my crypt and I did not earn a single
: victory point. My combat monsters watched helplessly as my predator's
: minions snuck past at +1 stealth.

: A rush deck that relies on BR/Ambush/HC and lacks *any* intercept ability is
: doomed to failure.

I see you have come here to stir up trouble. Happy to oblige. ;-)

You're right, a pure rush deck is a combo deck. However, to some extent,
just about every Jyhad deck is a combo deck. Whether your combo is '+bleed
cards and stealth' or 'damaging vote cards and presence vote enhancers'
or 'get into combat cards and damaging combat cards', you're still trying
to get multiple cards to work together so that your deck can be effective.

Many pure rush decks (eg potence/celerity rush combat) typically use larger
combos than other deck types (eg stealth bleed or ventrue presence vote)
for each successful action. But that doesn't mean they can't work. I
(and others) have experienced some tournament success playing pure rush
combat, in addition to regular group play. Not drawing a single rush
card is a problem I have almost never had. It's far more typical for
me to get hand-jammed on *too many* rush cards, because once I get into
a combat, it is usually possible to play many ephemeral combat cards,
whereas you can only play one rush card per action. I don't know why
you had the opposite problem, but I do think it's very feasible to play
pure rush decks that rarely (if ever) run into that particular difficulty.

In my experience, a primarily-rush combat deck with light intercept added
would do even worse against the stealth-bleed predator you describe. This
is because light intercept is usually not enough to consistently block
a stealth-bleed predator. So, your intercept cards produce no useful
effect, you have fewer rush cards available due to playing intercept
instead, and your predator is getting to cycle stealth cards because
you're trying to block. Now that's what I call a sticky situation.

Beast is a wonderful vampire. And a deck built around him may get
some utility out of being able to include fewer rush cards in the
library, because you can rely on his built-in ability. But a deck
that relies on library cards to get into combat *can* also work perfectly
well. The key is to put the right number of them in the deck, and it
is often a good idea to include some other extra card cycling to help
out in crunch situations.

Josh

The tournament that James's deck won was a 10 player tourney, and the only
thing special about it was that there were 3 Rush decks involved (James's,
Josh's, mine). Other than that, it was a pretty varied field of decks,
including Steve Wampler's killer Weenie Pre bleed deck that won the previous
Ithaca tournament. Another 10-12 player tournament that I attended a while
before the aforementioned one was won by a pure Rush deck of Josh's. My Marty
Lechtansi based Rush deck came in second (it actually had more total VPs than
Josh, but came in second to him in the finals). At Origins, my Rush deck
stacked up a good pile of VPs and got into the finals (and was killed by
seating there, as is the case with all final games). At Origins three years
ago, I played a Pot/Ani/Dom Rush deck that did very well, sweeping one table
and getting 1 VP in both of the other two games (and ended up getting ousted by
the person who won the tourney as I told her how to kill me--she was some
wizards employee who was playing with a borrowed deck so we could have 50
players--either she was a complete ringer, or I told her how to kill me...) As
these are pretty much the only four tournaments where we (James, Josh, myself)
have played good Rush decks, and we did very well in all four of them, I
suspect that it means something.

Not say that this is defenitive data to the fact that Rush decks are the best
decks in the world, but it is evidence that they _can_ win and _do_ win. I
maintain my theory that if more people understood how to play Rush decks, more
people understood how to design Rush decks, and more people played with Rush
decks, they would win more tournaments. I doubt that Josh, James, and I did as
well as we did simply on the strength of our genius and good looks alone.
There has to be something to this. Rush decks can and do work.

of the previously-viable rush decks. (This is something we talked about
at Origins a little, with Adrian Sullivan... he felt that the Rotschreck
change was good in turning the balance back toward making Tremere and
Gangrel intercept-combat playable again, (particularly in conjunction with
the Immortal Grapple one-round-only change); I felt that there was no
need to weaken IG combat considering that non-combat decks still are
easier to play and seem to win tourneys more often...)

: However, what i would REALLY like to see is a pool-gain card that does for

: successful combat what Voter Captivation and Legal Manipulation/Kindred
: spirits do for the voting and bleeding strategies respectively. eg "Spoils of
: Victory: combat card, playable when an opponent goes to torpor or is burned
: as a result of combat with this vampire. The vampire playing this card gains
: blood from the blood bank equal to the number of points of damage it
: inflicted on its opponent. Up to two of this blood can be diverted to your
: blood pool." Or else; "Triumph of the Beast: Action. Gain X pool, where X is
: the number of torpid vampires controlled by your prey." I think if we had
: cards like that there would be an EXPLOSION of creative rush decks of all
: different kinds.

Heh, heh, heh. This card (almost) already exists. It's called Anathema.
Yeah, it's a vote card, so clearly it's not going to fit into all combat
decks, but it can be Really Good. (I'm not sure now if we ever had
it outright banned, but I know we at least had a house rule that it could
only be called on a younger vampire for a while, due to people getting
tired of having me burn their vampires and gain lots of pool for it...)
(back in Ithaca, that was)

It's not as widely applicable as Voter Cap and Legal Manips, but then
those are both Presence cards (so they aren't universally usable either).
Anyhow, I would suspect that making pool-gain that easy for a combat
deck would have to be done pretty carefully to avoid imbalance. It's
already possible to do something like this via Taste of Vitae and
Blood Doll. I do like the idea, but Spoils of Victory might be a little
too good - compare to Taste of Vitae which doesn't get you any direct
pool gain and is already a very good card. Triumph of the Beast I like
more; there's no direct analogue to it, and also it rewards having your
prey's vamps in torpor, which works against the otherwise-desirable
course of burning them.

Josh
